fields.title: Go-to-market: decisions made before launch
fields.keyTakeaway: A launch is not the announcement day, but a set of decisions: who we sell to first, what we promise, how we sell, what support is ready for, and how we know it worked. The date comes last on this list.
fields.checkQuestion: The product is ready, the date is set. Which five decisions might be missing?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **what is needed for a successful launch?**
fields.blocks/1/subtitle: Four types of growth—and different levels of risk
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **Current product, current market**—deeper penetration. The cheapest and usually underused.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **Current product, new market**—a new segment or geography. The risk is that the task there is different, even if the product is similar.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: **New product, current market**—an expansion for those who are already with you. Clear channel, clear customer.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: **New product, new market**—the most expensive and most frequent place of failure: both sides are unknown at once.
fields.blocks/2/text: The **ADL approach** adds the question of maturity: in a young market, you win with speed and customer education; in a mature one, with efficiency and price. The exact same launch is done differently in these markets.
fields.blocks/3/title: Reestr launches a reconciliation statement module
fields.blocks/4/text: A wave of forty clients gives time to fix what was found. Announcing to the entire user base turns the first 24 hours into a lottery and makes any rollback public.
fields.blocks/4/title: Launching to everyone at once deprives you of the chance to learn
fields.blocks/5/text: A good launch does not save an unneeded product: it only speeds up getting an honest answer. If the answer is negative, the value of the launch is that you learned it in a month, not a year.
